## d22 batch106 BP1: fh wait while a belt_flow sample runs (Luna)

- Luna's request (shift60, 02:32): "Belt-flow measurement #49028604 is still active >100 seconds after requesting 30
  seconds; the wait action returns a stale completed gather rather than waiting."
- The journal (runs/shift60/luna/journal.jsonl, lines 192-273):
  - `belt_flow {position, seconds: 30}` at tick 49028604 (02:31:41Z), until_tick 49030404.
  - `fh call belt_flow` then read `belt_flow {}` each second (seconds_left 29 down to 1).
  - Two `fh wait` calls at 02:31:54 and 02:31:58 (`status {peek, brief}`, then a small observe) returned at once.
  - `stop` at 02:32:02; the sample went on (seconds_left 9 at the next read).
  - `belt_flow {}` at tick 49030406 (02:32:11Z) gave the result. At 60 UPS the sample ran its 30 s.
- Why: `fh wait` (host/cli.ts waitForIdle) waits on the character's action (status `active`, `combat`). A belt_flow
  sample is a bounded watch (measures.lua), not an action, so with nothing active the wait returned the last ended
  action. `stop` pauses the queue and ends the action and combat (runtime.lua handlers.stop); it does not touch a
  watch. A sample ends at its until_tick, or when a new `belt_flow {position}` replaces it.
- The change (CLI):
  - fh wait's polls ask for the watches: `status {peek, brief, work: true}`; a runtime that refuses `work` gets the
    polls as before.
  - With no action or combat running, and a `belt_flow` sample running that began after the last action ended, fh wait
    waits for the sample:
    - The budget is the sample's end tick, as for an action's; `--max` as given.
    - The wake rules are the same: a tell or mention ends it unless `--wait-through-tells` (`outcome: told`,
      `still_running: belt_flow sample ID, up to N s more`, exit 3), and an action begun meanwhile becomes what it
      waits for.
    - At the end it reads `belt_flow {}` once and gives its result, with `waited_for` (the watch id) and a note.
    - At the cap: `wait_timeout`, "your belt_flow sample ID is STILL SAMPLING ...", exit 3.
  - Any other watch running (uptime, turret_tally, collector_tally, asteroid_watch, flight_watch), or a sample begun
    before the action that ended: the reply has `watches` (their rows), and the note names each one: its id, end tick
    and seconds left, that no action or stop ends it, and the read that gives its result (`KIND {}`;
    `platform_supply {platform, collection: true}`, `platform_defense {platform, asteroids: true}`,
    `flight_watch {id: N}`).
  - Exit 3's stderr line for a sample says that no action or stop ends it (the action line's "a call that drives
    your character stops it" does not hold for a sample).
- belt_flow's start and progress replies have `ends`: "the sample ends at until_tick: stop and your actions do not end
  it (a new belt_flow {position} replaces it); fh wait waits for it when nothing else runs". Its help (returns) says
  the same.

## d22 batch110 BT1: the harness's garbage (Lua heap churn)

- The operator's profile of world n (20:24-20:25): the harness 3.95 ms a tick, the Lua heap growing 17.47 MB a second
  and falling in 5 of 61 seconds, those 5 the worst seconds (359-872 ms of harness work).
- Measuring who allocates (operator): `profile_ticks {seconds=N, alloc=true}` adds, per key at the end of the run,
  `agent-harness profile alloc ticks=T n=N key=K kb=KB gc_inside=G`: the heap grown inside each timed call
  (`collectgarbage("count")` before and after; a key's parts are inside it, and a call the heap fell in is counted in
  `gc_inside`, its growth not). `gc="stop"` stops the collector for the run and restarts it at the end, so nothing is
  freed inside a call and each count is what it allocated; the heap then grows by all of it for the run's seconds
  (keep runs short). The start reply's `collector` says the heap then, whether the collector ran and whether the stop
  was taken. `tools/profile_log.py` ranks the keys by MB, MB a second and KB a call. The timing wrapper itself makes
  about 1 KB a call.
- In 2.0.77 the harness's Lua state (Lua 5.2) takes `collectgarbage("count")`, `"isrunning"`, `"stop"` and `"restart"`
  (read on a copy of world n through the profiler).
- On a copy of world n's _autosave12 (d22 19:23), with shift60's usual calls replayed (per second 5 sleep_check
  observes over the 9 agents, 1.7 artillery_live operator reads, and status, platform, inspect, observe power and
  big_enemies_live at their journal rates), collector stopped for 20 s: the harness tick allocated 16.5 MB a second,
  scheduler.tick 5.3 MB of it.
  - Most of scheduler.tick was in the platform lanes' guards: Astra's Asterion lane (7 guards, among them two
    fluid_count) and Meridian-V and Anvil, checked every 10 ticks. fluid_count on a platform found every tank, pipe,
    thruster and machine aboard at each check (thousands of entity objects) and made a closure for each one; and
    reading an entity's method (`e.get_fluid_count`) makes a new function each time. 111 KB a check.
  - fluid_count now keeps a platform's holders and each one's `get_fluid_count` while their count
    (`count_entities_filtered`, no entity objects) is the same and each one kept is valid, and finds them again
    otherwise: the same entities and amounts as before, read live at each check. 4.5 KB a check (1 KB of it the
    profiler's).
  - With the same replay: the heap grew 15.60 MB a second before (main 88ba0901) and 11.98 after; the tick allocated
    16.5 and 11.2 MB a second, scheduler.tick 5.3 and 1.6.


### d22 batch109 BS1: flight watches, one per platform (#1952)

Sol #1952: the force limit of 8 flight watches kept Cinder's watch out while 18 platforms flew. Measured on a private
copy of world n's 19:23 autosave (`_autosave12`), which held 8 watches: 4 running, among them Asterion's (97 ammo turrets,
160 accumulators, 6743 belts), and 4 armed. The copy runs background work at world n's pace (batch96 BF1). Its JSON
encoding is about 30x slower than world n's, so a read's time below leaves the encoding out.

- Main's runtime, the save's 8 watches. Each watch's sample, per game second (median, mean, worst):
  - armed: 0.010-0.020 ms, mean 0.02-0.07;
  - a running watch on a small platform (9-10 turrets): 0.05-0.07 ms, mean about 0.1;
  - Asterion's: 0.47 ms, mean 0.72, worst 11.5 (it began an ammunition trace).
  - `flightwatch.tick`: 72 ms in the 60 s profile (1.2 ms a game second), all in one tick a second; worst second 5.8 ms.
- The cost of a running watch was its ammunition trace (ammofeed.lua), asked once a minute a watch:
  - On Asterion a trace finds its 6743 belts in the asking tick (8-79 ms), reads them in 27 background steps (median
    4.2 ms each), and ends in one tick (113 ms): about 510 ms a minute.
  - Petrel's 259 belts: 0.4-0.6 ms, 4 steps (6.8 ms), 4.4-5.7 ms to end.
  - The 18 platforms hold 12,327 belts. Traced once a minute each, that is about 15 ms a game second.
  - Spreading the find over the platform's 371 chunks costs 85 ms in all, against 21 ms for one find, so the trace's
    ticks are as they were.
- The change (flightwatch.lua):
  - Limit: one watch that counts per platform of the force (`limit`: 19 on the save, its 19 platforms, one without a surface yet). A watch counts while armed,
    watching, or done with its result not read. A done one read stops counting; it is kept 1 h as before, at most 16
    read ones a force (the oldest read dropped). A platform holds one counting watch as before (`replace: true`), and a
    replace is not refused at the limit. A start at the limit is refused with the count, the limit, the counting
    watches (`#id platform (state, setter)`) and how to end one: `flight_watch {id, clear: true}`, or read a done one.
  - `flight_watch {}` adds `limit`, `counted`, `counting` (ids), `limit_line` and `counts` on each row.
  - Ticks: each watch reads on its own tick of the second (`phase`: 51 first, then the least used in steps of 13); the
    tick hook asks `flightwatch.due(tick)` each tick. Each watch still reads once a second.
  - Feed traces:
    - A platform with no ammo turret asks none.
    - The periodic ask is once a minute, or once every 7 ticks a belt aboard if longer (Asterion: about 13 min).
    - A trace done since the last one taken is taken at the next sample (before, at the next ask).
    - The ask 10 s after a turret begins to read empty is as before.
    - The note says so; the trace's reply carries `belts`, and ammofeed has `done_tick`.
  - The armed check keeps the platform object, so it does not list the force's platforms each second.
  - Rows read the fuel held and in tanks alone (endurance `fuel_held`, the same figures as the fuel outlook's rows).
    The outlook's statistics, leg and speed were 12 ms of a 17.5 ms list of 18 watches.
  - The hub's repair packs are counted by a set of names, with no prototype read per stack.
  - runtime.lua times `ammofeed.step` as a profile part.
- After, the save's 8 watches: armed 0.009 ms a game second (worst 0.03-0.5); Asterion's 0.42 ms (worst 2.5), with no
  trace begun in the window.
- After, a watch on all 18 platforms (16 running, 2 done since), 60 s profile:
  - `flightwatch.tick`: 126 ms in all, 2.1 ms a game second over 17 ticks a second (0.13 ms a call); worst second 5.2
    ms, a garbage collection second.
  - `ammofeed.step`: 58 ms (1 ms a game second); worst second 38.9 ms, a trace ending on one tick.
  - Against the 16.7 ms tick, that is about 0.05 ms a tick on average for every watch together.
- Reads with 18 watches (copy, read time without encoding):
  - `flight_watch {}`: 15-17 ms before the fuel change, 9.5-11.8 after; 25.4 KB.
  - `{id}` on Asterion: 7.7-8.3 ms, then 6.0-6.3; 38.8 KB.
  - `{id}` on Kestrel II: 4.2-11.7 ms; 16.9 KB.
  - A start: 3.6-10 ms; 2.9-3.2 KB.
- Left over: a trace's end pass and its belt find each take one tick (Asterion 79 and 113 ms). A watch now begins one
  there every 13 minutes. Other readers (platform alerts under low ammo, the platform and endurance reads) ask on their
  own terms.
## d22 batch107 BQ1 (eng/d20-batch107): a delivery watch complete by receipt (Sol #1950)

Sol's watch #75 (10000 copper-plate from Spindle to the landing pad (74,208) on Fulgora, 20 minutes) read `late`
although all ten pods of 1000 were received by that pad: `reached` was a stock test only (the consumer holding `count`
more than at the start), and robots emptied the pad as the pods landed. On a headless copy of world n's 18:53 autosave
the watch's arrivals show the pad holding 1000, 1976, 2448, ... 5602 on each pod's landing tick, never 10000.

- delivery_watch keeps a running total of what the consumer received since the watch was set (delivwatch.lua; runtime
  deploy needed), apart from the last 16 `arrivals`. What counts:
  - a landing pad consumer: the pods that pad received;
  - a consumer aboard a platform: the pods its hub received;
  - a chest, silo or machine on a planet: the pods received by a landing pad in its logistic network on the tick each
    landed (robots carry it on from there); a pad in another network, or a pod landed with no pad, does not count.
  Only the pods the watch followed count (at most 32 followed at a time).
- When the total reaches `count` the watch is complete by receipt: state `received`, stage `received`. The setter
  hears "delivery watch #75 (...): received 10000 of 10000 in 10 pods by cargo-landing-pad (74,208) on fulgora since
  the watch was set, the last at tick 49028166, in time, 18m43s before the deadline; the stock test not met: the
  consumer holds 0 now (0 at the start), not seen holding 10000 more". The consumer's count is read on that pod's tick:
  holding `count` more then, the watch is `reached`, and that line names the received total too.
- Each pod line, the deadline line and the watch's `line` say "received N of count in P pods by ...", so `late`
  always shows how much was received. Row field `received {count, pods, last_tick, by, from_arrivals}`.
- A watch set before this deploy is counted once from its arrivals received by the pad or hub itself
  (`from_arrivals: true`).
- Headless copy, after a deploy: watch #75 read `received` (10000, 10 pods, by the pad, from its arrivals) within a
  second, with the line above. Cost: nothing new per tick; at a landing, a chest/silo/machine consumer adds two
  logistic network lookups (1.3 µs each on the copy).

## d22 batch117 BZ1 (eng/d20-batch117): platform_ammo_below, a platform's whole ammunition reserve (Astra #1970)

A full-edge abort must keep the return leg's ammunition. `item_count` with `platform` reads the hub alone and
`ammo_below` each turret alone, so no wait or guard could test the total aboard.

- New condition kind for `wait_until` and queue guards, in the body, remote and platform lanes (conditions.lua,
  ammoreserve.lua; runtime deploy needed): `platform_ammo_below {platform, item, count, quality?, max_age?}`.
  - `item`: an ammunition item. `quality`: as `item_count` (default normal; a quality name; "any" sums every quality;
    the item's name alone is normal quality only, checked on the copy).
  - The count is the item aboard in all places a player can open: the hub's main inventory, each ammo turret's ammo
    slots, each belt's transport lines (an underground exit's buried lines are its entrance's, counted once), each
    inserter's hand, each assembling machine's and furnace's output, each chest. Met below `count`.
  - `saw`: "platform Asterion: 5534 rocket aboard (hub 10, turrets 261, belts 5244, hands 6, machines 13) as read 12s
    ago (ticks 49811640-49811773: hub, 97 ammo turrets, 6743 belts, 289 inserters, 56 machines, 0 chests); met below 1".
- The reading is kept in the background (ammoreserve.lua), never read at a check: a check marks the platform as asked
  about, and a platform asked about within 10 min gets a pass begun every 30 s (1800 ticks), one pass at a time across
  platforms. A pass walks the platform's chunks one band a step (walk.lua, one chunk a band), reads at most 100 entities
  a tick, and reads the hub on its last step. Each entity is read once a pass, so nothing is counted twice within one
  reading. An item that moves between two places during the pass (about 2.2 s on Asterion) can be counted in both or
  in neither.
- Age and staleness (conservative, as Astra asked): age is ticks since the reading's pass began. With `max_age`
  (30..900 s, default 120) the condition is also met when the newest reading is older than max_age ("...; older than
  max_age 2m00s: met (stale reading)"), and when there is no reading max_age after the platform's first check. A guard
  on it therefore fires on a stale reading. While the first pass has not finished within max_age it is not met, and saw
  says so ("no reading of its ammunition yet (a pass began 0s ago; ...; met if none by max_age 2m00s)").
- A guard's baseline line names the background reading and max_age. The wait estimate label is "platform_ammo_below
  ITEM aboard PLATFORM" (it said "in PLATFORM hub").
- Measured on a headless copy of world n's 22:10 autosave (Asterion at Aquilo: 6743 belts with 14510 transport lines
  read, 289 inserters, 97 ammo turrets, 56 machines, no chest), with Astra's platform lane waiting on it:
  - `profile_ticks {seconds=60}`: `ammoreserve.tick` 323 ms over 60 s (0.09 ms a tick on average). That includes one
    second of 217 ms in which a garbage collection finished (the heap fell 71.6 MB). Without it, each pass took
    29 + 30 + 1.3 ms over three game seconds (about 0.5 ms a tick while it runs, 133 steps), and each second between
    passes about 0.14 ms (2 µs a tick). Over the 30 s cycle that is about 0.034 ms a tick.
  - The same pass run synchronously with the game paused: 49 ms in all. A one-tick full count by the same rules: 39 ms
    (find 4.8 ms, read 34.4 ms).
  - Against a full count: with the game paused, the pass's reading equalled a one-tick full count in every item,
    quality and place (rockets 5534; firearm-magazine 7173; railgun-ammo 2501). Running, three readings against a full
    count taken a few ticks after the check: 5534/5534, 5534/5534, 5532/5536.
- Tests: tests/d22_batch117.lua (arguments, first check, a pass by place and quality, the underground's buried lines
  once, the refresh after 30 s, stale and no-reading cases, the record dropped after 10 min, the remote and platform
  lanes' dry runs as a wait and a guard); tests/conditions.lua's quality refusal text updated.
## d22 batch116 BY1 (eng/d20-batch116): flight_watch in the remote and platform lanes (Astra #1968)

Astra's dry run of a full-edge plan (runs/shift60 full-edge-dry-run.json, lane `platform:Asterion`) refused its first
step: "steps[1] (flight_watch): action flight_watch is not supported in the remote lane (no body steps)". The watch
ends at the edge arrival, and the return-leg watch had to be started by hand.

- `flight_watch` runs as a step in the remote lane and in each platform lane (queue_lanes.lua; runtime deploy needed),
  as it ran in the body lane: it sets the harness's own watch, drives no character and changes no schedule. Dry runs
  accept it the same way.
- In lane `platform:NAME` a `flight_watch` step without `platform` and without `id` starts a watch on NAME (the step's
  args in the history then carry `platform`). `{}` in the remote lane lists the watches, as the direct call does.
- `replace: true` (flightwatch.lua) keeps the watch it replaces readable by `{id}`:
  - a done one (the outbound leg, ended "arrived at solar-system-edge") stays as it ended;
  - a watching one ends there, `ended_by` "replaced by #N", with its end totals taken;
  - an armed one (it never began) is dropped, as before.
  A kept one no longer counts against the limit, carries `replaced_by` (the new id) and `replaced_tick`, and is kept
  24 h unless read; once read it is kept 1 h after the read (at most 16 read or replaced a force, the oldest dropped).
  It no longer shows on the setter's card (status work rows).
- The start's reply adds `replaced_watch` (the replaced one's row without turret rows: id, state, ended_by, end_tick,
  replaced_by, line with leg, time watched, worst turret, damage, losses, repair packs and fuel) and `replaced_line`,
  e.g. "flight watch #1 on Asterion (ended: arrived at solar-system-edge) is kept: flight_watch {id: 1} reads it in
  full; it no longer counts against the limit; kept 24h00m00s unless read, then 1h00m00s after the read". For an armed
  one: "flight watch #N on X was waiting for its next departure: dropped, nothing read yet". `watch.replaced` is the id
  as before. A lane step's result keeps all of this in the queue history.
- Tests: tests/d22_batch116.lua (the dry run in both lanes, the default platform, a replace at the turnaround from a lane
  step and the full read after, a running and an armed one replaced, the card, a refused start at the limit);
  tests/d21_batch72.lua updated for the kept replaced watch.

## d22 batch118 CA2 (eng/d20-batch118): one whole-belt rule for inspect and circuit_audit, the game's

Viewer Aurora (site:4407): inspect said an `entire_belt_hold` reader reads "the whole belt followed through its
inputs and outputs" (a side-load ended the walk upstream, and a belt side-loading onto another went on into it);
circuit_audit said the game counts only the reader's belt segment. Both now walk the segment in `beltseg.lua`.

Measured on a private 2.0.77 server (a lab surface, items placed one per belt, readers wired to constant combinators,
game paused, two ticks run): a reader's signal was exactly the items of its segment. The segment ran through
straight belts, a corner, an underground pair and a belt tier change (transport to fast), and along the main line past
a side-load both ways; the belts side-loading onto it were a 2-tile segment of their own (a reader on one read only
those 2); a splitter ended it downstream, and a reader just past a splitter read its own segment only. A 300-belt
straight belt was one segment (300 read). Every belt of a segment reports one `total_segment_length` per lane; two
readers of one segment on one network double the signal.

On a copy of world n (Asterion, 47 wired readers), the item counts first differed for 36 readers. What the read sums
is each lane's transport lines of the segment: belt lanes, the lines under an underground pair (an entrance's lines 3
and 4; an exit's are one-tile lines of their own), and a splitter's lanes at the segment's ends on its side (lines
1-2 left input, 3-4 right input, 5-6 left output, 7-8 right output, as it faces; one splitter's other side was
another segment of the same length). Counted so, 42 readers match their wires exactly; the other 5 have other
sources on their networks (an arithmetic combinator's +10000, two readers on one network).

- inspect's `circuit.belt_segment`: the segment (belts, `total_segment_length`, where each end is and why), what its
  lines hold, the wires' read, and the rule in words.
- circuit_audit `{platform}`: `short_reads` and its lines name the belts in line past the segment's ends and where the
  segment ends; `double_counts` compares segments.
- Cost on the copy (emulated amd64): inspect's segment read of a 503-belt reader 4.2 ms (main 2.6); circuit_audit
  `{platform}` on Asterion 46.4 ms (main 41.3), one walk a reader.

## d23 batch123 CF2 (eng/d20-batch123): a watch split by an edit inside what it measures (mixed.lua)

Viewer Aurora (site:4494): "Could measurement watches flag module or feed edits during a test and mark the sample as
mixed? Preserve the before/after data and notify its owner to start a clean window." In shift63, Sonnet's module swaps
on Gleba breeders invalidated Luna's samples three times, and she reset each window by hand.

- What counts as an edit, for the bounded watches (uptime, turret_tally, belt_flow, collector_tally, asteroid_watch,
  and flight_watch while it watches):
  - Something done to a measured entity: built, mined, destroyed, configured, rotated or wired, or items moved in or
    out by a call or a ctrl-click.
  - A feeder of one built, removed or configured: an inserter or drill whose drop or pickup point is on it, a loader
    touching it, or a beacon whose supply area reaches it.
  - For belt_flow: a belt, splitter, loader or inserter within a tile of the sampled line's box.
  - On a watched platform: any turret, collector, thruster, beacon, inserter, loader or belt.
- Where edits are seen:
  - The harness's builds and mines, and the configure, rotate, transfer, feed, refuel, rearm and wire calls of any
    agent.
  - The events control.lua forwards: on_built_entity, the mined events, on_entity_died, on_player_fast_transferred,
    and on_gui_opened/closed when the recipe or modules differ between them.
  - Not seen: construction robots' and platforms' own builds (no event of them is forwarded).
  - A second edit of the same entity in the same tick counts once.
- What happens at the first edit and each one after:
  - The watch's read up to the edit is kept: `mixed.parts` holds from_tick, to_tick, line, and up to 64 lines.
  - The watch starts again from the edit tick with its first arguments, to the same end tick. A flight watch's counts
    begin again, to its arrival or limit.
  - The watch ends at the edit instead, its final being that part, in three cases: an entity it measures was mined or
    destroyed, the new start is refused, or fewer seconds are left than a new watch takes.
- Where it shows:
  - `mixed.edits` gives each edit's tick, what was done, by whom, on which entity, and how it touches the watch.
  - The watch's read (`uptime {}`, `turret_tally {}`, belt_flow, platform_supply's tally, platform_defense) has
    `mixed`. The watch row (status work, idle, sleep) adds the line.
  - The owner hears it once in team alerts.
- The copy of world n (10:10 save): Grok's uptime on biochambers (54.5,58.5) and (52.5,48.5) ran 12 s. Then Grok's
  configure of 4 speed-module-2 into (54.5,58.5) split it. The read kept the 12 s part, with 9 completions over the two
  machines, and the new window ran from the configure's tick.
- Costs on the copy (emulated amd64, no tick work):
  - An index rebuild after a watch starts or splits: 0.76 ms.
  - The running-watch check with stored watches: 0.13 ms.
  - An edit of ours that touches no watch: 0.29 ms; with no watch stored: 0.004 ms.
  - A death of another force's entity is dropped at the force check.

## d23 batch123 CF3 (eng/d20-batch123): supply left without an active delivery path (freightpath.lua)

Viewer Aurora (site:4495): "Could disabling a freight request or retiring a route flag any essential supply left without
an active delivery path, naming the missing link and owner? Please test the bioflux case."

- A delivery path of an item to a planet has two ends:
  - A platform whose hub requests the item (an active section, minimum above 0) from an import planet its schedule
    stops at.
  - A planet the schedule also stops at, whose landing pad requests the item.
- The calls checked: `requests` on a hub or landing pad that changes slots or sections, `platform_schedule`, and
  `platform_delete` (a platform scheduled for deletion has no paths). Each reads the paths before and after.
- Which items are read:
  - A hub's or platform's call: the items its hub asks now.
  - A pad's call: the items the pad asks now.
  - Only the hubs that ask one of them have their schedule and sections read (the game's compiled hub requests carry no
    import planet).
- Each item and planet that had a path and has none is a `supply_left` line. It names the paths it had and the link
  each lost (the pad's request, the hub's request, a stop, the platform deleted). It also gives who set that link last
  before the call (`editlog.owner`: the newest edit of that section or the schedule before this tick, or "no earlier
  editor recorded"), the planet's use in the last 10 minutes, and its pad's stock. That editor, when someone else, gets
  one tell; `supply_left_told` names them.
- The bioflux case on the copy (10:10 save). Cinder and Meridian-V request bioflux from Gleba (40 each) and stop at
  Nauvis. Nauvis's pad section 6 asks bioflux 20; it was off in the save, so it was turned on first. Then:
  - Astra turned off section 6: "bioflux to nauvis: no active delivery path left; it had Cinder from gleba, Meridian-V
    from gleba; nauvis's landing pad no longer requests bioflux (set last by opus at tick 52085722); nauvis used 10 in
    the last 10 minutes; nauvis holds 0 in its landing pad". Opus was told. Tick 52085722 is Opus's clear of the pad's
    bioflux at 16:58.
  - With the pad back on, turning off Meridian-V's section 23 left Cinder's path: no line. Then turning off Cinder's
    section 1 gave "... it had Cinder from gleba; Cinder's hub no longer requests bioflux from gleba (set last by sol
    at tick 49459484) ..." (Sol told).
  - Cinder's schedule cut to Gleba alone gave "Cinder's schedule no longer stops at nauvis (no earlier editor
    recorded)".
- Costs on the copy:
  - A pad call (the pad asks 40 items, 15 hubs read): 3.8 ms a read, two reads a call, plus 0.15 ms for the paths and
    their difference.
  - A Meridian-V call (2 items): 1.1 ms a read.
  - The whole pad call, the request edit included: 15-17 ms.
  - Reading every hub's sections (before the narrowing) took 6.5 ms; the pads come from the census.

## d23 batch123 CF4 (eng/d20-batch123): one scan call's work bounded

Operator 10:25. In the world n profile of 10:17-10:18, `observe {scope: scan}` ran 22 calls at 96 ms each on average.
The worst game second was 670 ms, from 4 scans, and the 3 worst seconds of the minute were all scans. They were Sol's,
17:17:53-17:17:58Z: Asterion in 16-tile bands (area 112x16; belts, splitters, ammo turrets, inserters and assemblers;
fields inventory; limit 1024).

On a copy of world n (10:10 save), the y=32 band held 697 candidates (669 belts). Finding them took 0.5-0.8 ms. Its
call took 166 ms with no fields and 346-519 ms with inventory. Three costs, each fixed with the facts per row unchanged
(the inventory band's reply is the same 74,433 bytes before and after):

- `fields: inventory` asked all 29 inventory names of each entity through a refused pcall. A belt failed every one,
  then read its lanes. It now asks only the inventories its type takes, in the same order (`M.scan_inventories`,
  memoised by type). The band went from 346-519 ms to 103 ms.
- With `platform=` the caller is a remote-view stand-in, and each `p.surface` or `p.force` read went through it. The
  candidate loop (known, hidden_own) read them several times for each of the 697. They are now read once a call. The
  band at `limit: 1` went from 70 ms to 21 ms.
- The sorts read each row's position and name about 20 times. They are now read once a row, and each row's type and
  force once.
- Encoding the reply took about 39 ms of the band's 100 ms. Rows now come 256 a call (`M.SCAN_PAGE`) in reading order:
  `page`, `pages`, `rows` ("257..512 of 697") and, before the last, `more {rows, next {page}, line}`; `page: N` with the
  same arguments lists the next. A scan keeping 256 rows or fewer reads as before.

Sol's 18 band calls on the copy, every page, same load (host load average 12-14):
- Main's runtime: 18 calls, 3.78 s in all, 97-353 ms a call (210 ms on average).
- This branch: 38 calls (pages), 1.39 s in all, 36 ms a call on average, 25-56 ms for a full 256-row page, with one
  129-220 ms outlier band in a run under load.
- The copy reads about 2.2 times world n's cost for these calls (210 against 96 ms on average), so a full page should
  be near 20-25 ms on world n.
## d22 batch122 CE1 (eng/d20-batch122): a reply closes only what it answers, for teammates too

Viewer Aurora (08:48): "can an unrelated reply to someone clear their other unanswered requests?" It could, for
teammates. batch57 S1 had held a viewer's lines to closing by name only while one was open, but for a teammate:
- a say or team tell naming the sender closed every open request of theirs, with or without `reply_to`;
- any tell to them closed all of theirs, including a tell with `reply_to` to one of them.

Case (tests/d22_batch122.lua, through the runtime): Sol asked Muse two things; Muse's `say {reply_to: <the second>,
text: "@sol yes, sending 50 plates now."}` closed both.

Now (owed.lua, board.lua, tells.lua), the same rule for viewers and teammates:
- `reply_to` on a say or tell closes exactly the lines it names.
- Without it, a say or team tell naming the sender, or a tell to them, closes their line only while it is their one
  open line to you.
- A say's or tell's `left_open` names the senders it left several open lines of: "sol has 2 open requests to you
  (#11, #12): a say or tell naming them closes none; reply_to closes the one it names".
- The unanswered line for a teammate reads "reply_to: 11 answers it (a say or tell naming sol, or a tell to them,
  does while it is their only open request)".

## d22 batch122 CE2: board progress tells repeated sleeps from waits and rests (viewer Aurora site:4485)

Before, a board item's 10-minute check (progress.lua) read "waiting (sleep)" whenever its owner was in an fh sleep,
and the unchanged count stood still: an agent sleeping in repeated 300 s sleeps with no progress kept its items
"waiting" for ever, never stalled. A quota rest (rests.lua) read "stalled". A board_focus on a task (no step) never
flagged. Now the runtime gives the owner's wait a kind:
- a wait on something (wait_until, a sleep with a game condition, a running queue or its wait step): "waiting
  (wait_until)", "waiting (sleep until item_count)"; the count holds;
- a rest: "resting until 15:59 (quota)"; the count holds;
- a sleep with no game condition, or a direct wait_ticks: the count goes on, said beside it: "stalled: unchanged across
  2 checks (its owner in a sleep on no game condition at this check; at 1 of these 2)".
A focus on the item alone counts its unchanged checks by the same rule: "the focused item shows no progress across 2
checks". board_critical's agents line gives the same wait text. The idle nudge (tools/idle_nudge.py) and supervise.sh
were checked with the same cases: repeated sleeps, wait_until and wait_ticks are nudged with the wait named ("sleeping 5
min", "in wait_until"), a rest in resting.json is skipped ("out of quota until Sat 09:25"); unchanged.

## d22 batch122 CE2: nutrient accounting, fuel, spoiling, time windows and stock scope (viewer Aurora 10:13)

Measured on a private 2.0.77 copy of world n's 10:26 save:
- spoiling counts on neither side of the production statistics: 100 nutrients spoiled in a chest read used 0, and
  spoilage made 0;
- fuel counts as used when a burner takes it from its fuel slot (a biochamber's 5 nutrients: used 5);
- a productivity bonus's extra products count as made, ingredients only for the crafts run; a returned catalyst
  (pentapod-egg: 1 in, 2 out) counts on neither side, so an egg craft at +50% reads 1.5 made;
- the ten-minute flow read (count) matched the running totals' difference over the same 10 minutes within 0.2%
  (40,509 against 40,585 made over 36,045 ticks);
- Gleba, 10 game minutes: nutrients made 40,585 and used 34,943 (egg recipes 2,992 a minute, biochambers' fuel about
  500 a minute); every place held 3,758 then 3,704, so 5,696 (569 a minute) spoiled. That is the positive balance.

Before: supply, stock, freight_audit, fuel_budget and dependency gave made above used with no word of spoiling;
supply's `where` left out fuel slots (195 of Gleba's 3,792) and the ground; stock counts networks, chests, pads, silos
and labs (2,687); dependency read nutrients "sustained" and took the egg crafts as 74.6 a minute (made / 2), 99.7
measured.

Now (spoilflow.lua):
- supply `flow` of an item that spoils says what the statistics leave out; a read of the whole surface keeps its count,
  and the next one 1-60 min later gives `uncounted`: "over the last 5 min (whole-surface counts at tick T and now): made
  20120, used 17445; held 3758 then, 3770 now; 2663 left uncounted (532.6 a minute): spoiled, or carried off the
  surface". `where` adds fuel slots (machines, heating towers, boilers, burner drills, vehicles) and, read whole, the
  stacks on the ground as the ground watch last binned them.

  last measure (at most 30 min old) a minute.
- dependency: an ingredient that spoils is short or not sustained by made - used - what left uncounted a minute, when
  supply measured it; otherwise the last line names it as not counted. The crafts run: made over what the statistics
  count a craft (products past a returned catalyst, with the makers' average productivity bonus from the census).
Regression: tests/d22_batch122b.lua.
- cp2: the background jobs' per-entity garbage, module by module (the same facts; each module's tests, and new
  tests/d22_batch110_misc.lua and tests/d22_batch110_freight.lua comparing kept and fresh reads):
  - walk.lua: one filter and area table for every band; the band is the find's own list with the entities outside it
    taken out; an optional out_pos hands each entity's position (as the band read it) to the caller, so survey,
    pushalerts and census read no position again.

    name, as machine_status gives it; a burner one burnt.stuck once, not twice); each read once an entity; no

  - pushalerts.lua: guarded reads through shared getters (no closure a read; 5-10 an entity before); an entity's type,

    before its recipe is read; output_chest_full and catalyst_gone ran a second time untimed when they found nothing:
    once now; inserter records rewritten in place; prototype facts cached by name. lightning.lua: a building's
    position read once.
  - census.lua: positions from the band; a recipe read once; no closures; the step's lookups kept between steps.

  - conditions.lua: ammo_below and platform_energy_below on a platform keep their turret and accumulator lists as

  - threat.lua, spoil.lua, platalerts.lua, flightwatch.lua: scratch tables reused, force, surface and platform kept

### d22 batch113 BW1: a teammate covering a resting owner's claim

Viewer Aurora (21:31): "Could factory digests follow temporary ownership? Sonnet is covering Gleba, but its alerts went
to Grok on quota rest while Sonnet got Vulcanus updates." Grok's account hit its weekly limit at 20:04. Grok rests until
Sat 16:00 (rests.lua; batch108), and Astra arranged at 20:06 for Sonnet to cover Gleba.

- What happened (runs/shift60; the board and alerts on a copy of world n's autosave from about 21:24):
  - Grok's last request was at 20:03:59. It has received nothing since: alerts to it wait unseen.
  - Grok's claim #1130 "Gleba science, breeder, cultivator" covers (-16,8)-(36,56) on Gleba. The 6 alert groups
    there went to grok alone:
    - 31 logistic containers that lost their source;
    - 3 machines held off by their conditions;
    - a catalyst gone;
    - deliveries waiting;
    - a full output chest;
    - a full requester.
  - 7 more Gleba groups went to grok as the nearest agent: its character stands on Gleba nearer than Sonnet's.
  - The claim was 81 min without Grok's activity, so it closes at 2 h (about 22:04). Its groups then go by builder
    or nearness, which is Grok again.
  - The 21:28 factory digest sent its Gleba blockers to grok, since #1130 is the only claim on Gleba
    (tools/factory_digest.py `owners`).
  - Sonnet (20:06-21:36): 129 distinct alert lines.
    - 47 name Gleba: 35 platform arrivals and departures, heating towers, eggs, coverage. Some Gleba groups outside
      #1130 came as the nearest agent then.
    - None came from inside #1130.
    - Sonnet holds #1961 (a request on Gleba calcite) and no claim on Gleba.
- What routes by claim owner:
  - pushalerts `owners` (team alerts, game_alerts' `to`, sleep levels): claims over a group's centre or a boiler's
    feed chest, else builders, else the nearest agent; ammo_low by builders and agents within 64 tiles.
  - urgent.lua `my_claim`: losses in a fresh claim of yours wake a sleep, as do outposts' drills.
  - tools/factory_digest.py `owners`: claims holding a fact's positions, else every claim on the surface, else the
    holders of items that name it.
  - The board's own claim news goes to the owner.
  - alertdigest.lua and platdigest.lua do not route by owner.
- What the board had: a claim stays with its poster (board_update refuses `owner` on a claim). `allow` names agents whose
  stock sweeps include it, the owner's call only. Nothing let a teammate hear a claim's alerts.
- The change: one argument of an existing action, `board_update {id, cover: true|false}`:
  - Who: any agent but the owner and the operator, on an active claim; at most 4 coverers.
  - The claim keeps `covers` [{name, since}], shown on the board and in its label ("covered by sonnet").
  - A note says "sonnet covers it: hears its alerts with grok (resting until Sat 16:00 (quota))", or "sonnet no longer
    covers it".
  - A coverer hears the claim's alert groups with its owner (pushalerts `owners`: why `covers`). Its line ends
    "(claim #1130 by grok, resting until Sat 16:00 (quota); you cover it)".
  - A coverer's sleep wakes for losses in it: "buildings destroyed in claim #6 "iron" by opus, which you cover".
  - The factory digest sends the claim's facts to its coverers too (the board read's `covers`).
  - A coverer counts as allowed (stock sweeps), and its requests in the area and its updates on the claim keep the
    claim fresh, as the owner's do. So a covered claim does not close while the coverer works there.
  - For as long as it is set, not only while the owner rests. The owner keeps hearing everything, so a cover takes
    nothing away. A rest ends by itself at the owner's first request or its tick, which says nothing of whether the
    owner is back on that area. The agents set and clear the cover; the harness never picks a coverer.
- Where the team reads an alert routed to a resting owner:
  - The teammates line (status): "Grok (resting until Sat 16:00 (quota); 13 alert groups go to it (claim #1130 6,
    nearest 7), heard by no one else)". Once Sonnet covers it: "...; also heard by sonnet (covers) 6; 7 by no one
    else". Read from the last scan, kept a second.
  - game_alerts `to`: "grok (claim; resting until Sat 16:00 (quota))", "grok (nearest; resting until ...)",
    "sonnet (covers claim #1130 by grok)".
  - The factory digest's team part: "to agents resting: grok (resting until Sat 16:00 (quota)): N facts went to it;
    sonnet got M" (or "to no one else"). Read from runs/RUN/AGENT/resting.json, as tools/stream/pacing.py reads it.
- Not changed: the nearest-agent rule still names a resting agent (7 of Gleba's groups at 21:24). The teammates line
  and game_alerts now say so; choosing someone else there would pick for the agents.
- On the copy (copy of the 21:24 save, paused): status by astra takes 11.1-11.4 ms on the branch against 11.2-12.0 on
  main, warm. game_alerts on Gleba (18.3 KB) takes 12.7 ms.

## d22 batch122: wire sides in the dry run, enclosed foundation laid live, quality in inspect and scan (Astra #2087, 18:18)

Astra's collector line on Asterion: the place_ghosts dry run at tick 53751814 read `dry_run_ok` with two green wires
from a fast belt given `from_side: "output"`, and counted 32 foundation tiles, 17 under the ghosts and 15 holes. The live
call at 53827409 refused both wires (`from_side applies to combinators only (and power switches for copper)`) and laid
only the 17 under its ghosts; two ghosts stayed unbuilt until the 15 holes were placed by hand at 53828751.

Wires. The dry run now checks each entry wire's two ends by the live wire's own rules (circuits.lua `wire_end_id`, which
`wire` itself now calls): the entry, and at `to` an entry of the same call whose footprint holds it, else what stands
there. Each wire gets a row in `settings_check` (`green to (x,y): ok`, or the live call's refusal), counts in
`settings_refused`, and a refused one fails the verdict. A combinator's sides, a power switch's `left`/`right` for copper,
a pole's single copper connector and an entity with no circuit connection are judged as the live call judges them.

Foundation. The live call collects every tile ghost it lays on a platform (under its ghosts and its own tile entries) and
runs the dry run's hole flood from them (dryrun.lua `enclosed`, now shared; `live_holes` reads the surface as it stands,
tile ghosts counting as foundation). The enclosed tiles get tile ghosts too, counted in `tiles_laid`, with `holes_laid`,
`holes_note` and `holes_failed` (a refused one, with why). The largest region the new tiles part may still stay empty,
as the dry run says (`holes_other`).

## d22 batch122: a new tile joined to the floor by a corner (Astra #2089, 19:36)

Astra's dry run of two laser turrets on Asterion (tick 54117906, at (-23,-48) and (23,-48)) read `dry_run_ok` while
`tiles.not_connected` said their 8 foundation tiles touch no existing foundation and stay unbuilt. Each turret's tiles
met the floor only at a corner. The two checks disagreed: `not_connected` followed sides only, while the hub's rules
played over the plan (`tiles.unbuilt`) build a tile with foundation among the 8 round it. On a 2.0.77 copy of world n
(its 18:24 save) the live call laid the 8 tile ghosts and the hub built all 8 within about 1200 ticks, so the play and
the verdict were right and `not_connected` was not.

Now `not_connected` follows sides and corners, and counts its tiles in `not_connected_count`. A tile it names fails the
verdict (`N foundation tiles the hub never builds: no foundation by a side or a corner, even through the other new tiles
(tiles.not_connected)`) when the play did not already count it in `unbuilt_count`, as when the floor is too large for
one tick and is checked across ticks. The summary says it too. An ok verdict over a floor not checked yet now says so:

On the copy with this branch: a laser turret at (-27,-48), whose tiles meet the floor only at (-26,-47), read ok and the
hub built its 4 tiles; one at (-27,-52), a tile away from any foundation, read `fails: 4 foundation tiles the hub never
builds ((-27.5,-52.5): no foundation among the 8 tiles round it)`, and its 4 tile ghosts were still unbuilt about 4770
ticks after the live call. Regression: tests/dryrun.lua (the #2089 block: corner contact, a square one tile apart, and
the verdict over a floor not played), failing on the old dryrun.lua and runtime.lua.

## d23 batch132 PD1: what a pad asked when a pod left the hub, and its on-the-way count (Sol #2093)

Sol's case: Kestrel IVc stopped at Gleba with 1500 processing units, Gleba's landing pad (54,8) had section 12 asking
`processing-unit 300..300`, and two pods came down, 1000 and 300. When Sol read the pad, section 1 (set by the circuit
network) asked only `foundry 3..inf`.

On a 2.0.77 copy of world n (its 20:45 save, 12 minutes before Sol's drop) with Sol's steps replayed:

- The pad's section 1 is set by a decider combinator at (65,24.5): for each item, it outputs the target on its green
  input when its red input (target less the stock of the logistic network the arithmetic combinator reads) is above
  0. The targets include `processing-unit=1000`. From tick 54474024 the network held under 1000 processing units,
  and section 1 asked `processing-unit 1000..inf`.
- Section 12 went on at 54478890. Kestrel IVc reached Gleba at 54488819 and in that tick sent two pods to the pad:
  1000 and 300 processing units, the pad's 1300 asked less the 0 it held (its trash, 16 then, does not count).
  The pad's requester point counted 1300 on the way from then to the landing.
- The 300 landed first (54489991); section 12 went off; three ticks later the network held over 1000 again and
  section 1 dropped processing units. The 1000 landed at 54490008 with no section asking for it, and most of it went
  to the pad's trash.

What is new in the reads:

- Each landed receipt in platforms `landed` says what the planet's landing
  pad asked of the pod's cargo when the pod left the hub, as the pad's window showed it then: each active section
  asking it with min..max and whether the circuit network sets it, what the pad held, what the other pods followed to
  that planet carried of it, and the pad's own on-the-way count. On the copy: `processing-unit*300 received by
  cargo-landing-pad (54,8) on gleba, ...; when it left the hub the pad asked processing-unit 1300 (section 1, set by
  the circuit network: 1000..inf; section 12: 300..300), held 0, 1000 on the way in pods followed`.
- `requests` on a landing pad returns `on_the_way`: what the pad counts as coming down to it (item*count), or
  `nothing`. On the copy it read `iron-plate*100 (cargo pods coming down to it)` for the 1150 ticks a pod flew.

Read only: nothing changes what the hub sends.

## d24 batch137 PI1: what a platform hub keeps at a stop (Sol #2107)

Sol's Petrel at Nauvis held 1980 calcite with sections calcite 200..inf from nauvis, 0..inf from gleba and 2000..2500
from vulcanus; the pad asked 2000; nothing went down, while shipment's ready read said 1776 would. Measured on a 2.0.77
copy of world n (d24, the save of that moment; Petrel and Petrel III at Nauvis, calcite, a manual pad request of 2000):

| Hub calcite sections (active) | Pad asks | Kept | Went down |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200..inf from nauvis (+ gleba 0..inf, vulcanus 2000..2500) | 2000 | all 1980 | 0 |
| 200..200 from nauvis (the same others) | 2000 | 200 | 1780 (1500 to the pad, 286 through the hub's trash) |
| gleba 0..inf and vulcanus 2000..2500 only | 2000 | what the pad did not ask | what the pad lacked |
| 200..500 from nauvis | 2000 | 500 | 1480 |
| 100..300 and 200..400, both from nauvis | 2000 | 700 | 800 |
| none | 2000 | 0 | all |
| 200..500 from nauvis | none | 500 | 1000 of 1500, to the pad |
| none | none | all | 0 |

So at a stop: only active sections importing from that planet count (a slot always names a planet: one set with none
read vulcanus); their maxes add up; an infinite max keeps it all whatever the pads ask; a finite max sends down all
above it to the pad there, whether the pad asks or not; an item no such section names goes down as far as the pads ask
(their ask less what they hold). The minimum plays no part in what goes down.

freight.lua `hub_keeps_at` and `hub_gives` state that rule, and every read that predicts a drop uses it: shipment's
ready read (`the hub would send down ...`, now with the section that keeps the rest, and `kept aboard: calcite: none
of 1500 (hub section 4 keeps calcite 200..inf at nauvis; the pads ask 2000, hold 0)`), shipment's cargo conflict
lines, the platform read's freight stop lines (`expected down`), the requests dry run's `sends_down`, and
delivery_watch's risks and blockers for the stops before the destination (a finite max there is a risk with no pad
asking). On the copy, Petrel III with calcite 200..inf from nauvis read kept aboard as above, and with 200..200 read
`the hub would send down calcite 1300 (... all above 200: hub section 4 keeps calcite 200..200 at nauvis, ...)`.

## d24 batch136 PH1 (eng/d20-batch136): signals named on inspect and circuit_audit (Sol #2104)
- Sol and Luna needed signal-R on red network 1258 at the native quota decider (51.5,48) on nauvis. The network carried
  242 signals. inspect lists 30 a network (`more` past them) and circuit_audit 24 (`signals_total`), so R was not in
  either list, and its absence could not be told from the cut.

  and the other typed forms, or `{type, name, quality}`. Give a list, or one string with `|` or `,`. A name the game
  doesn't have is refused. Each name is read with the network's own get_signal: the count the game holds, 0 when
  absent, whatever the cap.

  - `circuit_audit {area | positions, signals}`: each network row adds `picked`, and its line adds `named: ...`.
    circuit_audit reads, as before, the networks on an entity's red and green circuit connectors (a combinator's input
    side). `signals` with `platform` alone is refused.
  - `signals`, `more`, `signals_total` and the lines' `(+N more)` are unchanged.

## d24 batch138 PJ1 (eng/d20-batch138): queue_submit start:false stages the steps (Sol #2111)
- Petrel's lane (`platform:Petrel`, revision 452) was empty and not paused. `queue_submit {mode: replace, start: false}`
  queued revision 453, and its first step, `platform_schedule {paused: false}`, ran, then the arrival wait, without
  `queue_resume`. start:false only skipped the unpause, so on a lane that was not paused the steps ran at once.
- Now `start: false` pauses and holds the lane in the same call, as `queue_pause` holds it, whatever its state was. This
  holds on every lane (body, remote, platform:NAME) and in every mode (append, replace, ahead, next, pending). An active
  step is stopped and requeued at the head, as queue_pause does. Nothing the call submitted runs until `queue_resume`.
  Direct calls ending do not resume it (resume_direct, resume_after and the requeued-load resume skip a held queue).
  - The reply adds `staged`, e.g. `start: false: the lane is paused and held until queue_resume (it was not paused);
    2 steps pending`, and every queue_submit reply adds `state`: `running`, `paused`, or
    `paused, held until queue_resume`. queue_status's `paused_by` says `staged by queue_submit start: false`.
  - `start` must be true or false. A submit with start omitted or true runs as before.
- Other ways steps could start unasked, checked in the code:
  - A direct call ending: scheduler.resume_direct, runtime.resume_after and resume_requeued_load all skip a held queue.
  - A finished wait: the scheduler's tick advances only lanes not paused, and the pause clears the active step.
  - A runtime deploy: carry.lua snapshots only lanes not paused before it, so a held lane is not resumed.
  - Standing orders: run_order needs a free queue (no active step, nothing pending, no loop).
  - Shift start: research.lua's shift_start does not touch queues.
  - The tools: idle_nudge.py and idle_report.py only read; no tool sends queue_resume.
- Test: tests/d24_batch138.lua (fails on main: platform_schedule ran without queue_resume).


## d24 batch140 PL1 (eng/d20-batch140): signal_watch, a bounded watch of named circuit signals (Sol #2116)
- Petrel's zero-hub trial 1177 needed the whole-loop calcite minimum on belt (-13.5,4.5)'s green network 815 through
  flight and coasting. flight_watch reads fuel and ammunition, an inspect now and then can miss a brief low, and a
  queue's inspect reads one moment.
- `signal_watch {position, surface | platform, wire, side?, signals, seconds, reason?}` (signalwatch.lua, measures kind
  `signal_watch`): the network on one entity's `wire` (red or green); `side` (input or output) only on an arithmetic,
  decider or selector combinator, and required there. `signals`: 1..8 names as inspect's `signals` takes them
  (batch136: `name@quality`, `recipe:NAME`, `{type, name, quality}`, a list or one string with `|` or `,`).
  `seconds`: 10..3600. Refused: no network on that wire, an unknown name, a side on an entity with one side.
- A sample at the start and every 60 ticks after: one get_signal per signal (0 when absent, as the wire's hover shows).
  Nothing is read between samples.
- `signal_watch {}` reads it so far (`watching`) or done (`done`; the first read after the end is its final read):
  - `signals [{name, start, end, min, max, line}]`, each `{count, tick}`; min and max are the first tick that count was
    seen, and on a platform `where` it was then (`flying nauvis-gleba, 30 km/s`, `at gleba, 0 km/s`), read only on a
    sample that set a new min or max;
  - `samples`, `missed`, `gaps [{why, from_tick, to_tick, missed}]` and `gap_lines`: no network on that wire (a wire cut,
    its network gone) over a span of samples, and `network changed: #815 to #902` at the tick it was seen (samples go
    on reading the new network); 32 kept, `gaps_more` past them;
  - `ended {tick, why}`: the entity or its surface gone; the watch ends there;
  - `line`, `note` (a count held under 60 ticks can fall between two samples).
- One watch an agent: a new one replaces it (`replaced` names it). It is the agent's work while it runs, as the other
  bounded watches are: status {brief, work} rows, the idle check, the sleep line. No walk, no queue stop.
- Test: tests/d24_batch140.lua (refusals, sides, one get_signal per signal a sample and none between, a wire cut and a
  network change, where the platform was at the min, the status row, the end and the entity gone).
## d24 batch143 PO1 (eng/d20-batch143): the collector tally counts what the collectors caught (Sol #2133)
- Sol's collector_tally on Limestone reported 7 metallic as "collected" in 86 s. Its collectors take only oxide and
  carbonic, and its carbonic reprocessing crusher made 22 crafts. The platform's production statistics count every
  chunk made on the platform. Reprocessing returns carbonic 0.4, metallic 0.2 and oxide 0.2 a craft, and advanced
  crushing returns its chunk 0.05.
- 2.0.77 has no catch counter, checked on a copy of world n's 03:27 save. No collector or platform attribute answers:
  products_finished, collected and the like read missing, and the platform has none either. No event names a collected
  chunk: the space-platform events are built/mined/changed_state only. The arm inventory reads nil.
- caught: each collector's output count by chunk type, and the hands of the inserters taking from it (pickup_target the
  collector, found within 4 tiles, rechecked every 600 ticks; a new one's hand is no pickup). A chunk arrived is the
  output's rise plus the chunks its inserters picked up since the last read (a hand empty at one read and holding at
  the next). Chunks stack to 1, so a pickup is one chunk. Reads come every read_every ticks: under half the shortest
  half turn of those inserters, at most 10 (normal fast inserters at 0.04 turns a tick: every 6). An output that falls
  with no pickup is `taken_otherwise` (robots, a hand), not caught.
- Measured on the copy, Asterion (17 collectors, 14 crushers, in flight):
  - A level-script ground truth read every tick: over 16,359 ticks the platform made 336 carbonic, 273 metallic and
    707 oxide. The collectors' outputs received 229, 186 and 508, and the crushers' outputs 106, 88 and 197. Made
    equalled the two together within 9 a type at every read (the counts' timing), so a third of what was made there
    was the crushers' returns. Reads every 6 ticks gave the same catch as every tick.
  - The watch on this runtime over 4467 ticks: caught 56 carbonic, 36 metallic and 174 oxide, the same as the ground
    truth. Made was 366, 100 more than caught; the crushers put out 101.
- Cost, with profile_ticks over 60 s of the watch on Asterion: collector_tally.tick took a median 0.161 ms a tick on
  main's runtime and 0.190 ms on this one (17 collectors, 17 inserters). That is about 0.17 ms per catch read every
  6 ticks. The work per read is one output count per collector (its per-type counts only when it changed or an
  inserter picked up) and one hand per inserter, for one platform per watch and one watch per agent.
- platform_supply {collection: true}: `collected` is now `made`, said as the production statistics, every chunk made
  on the platform with the crushers' returns among them. The line reads `made on Limestone (production statistics:
  every chunk made on the platform, the crushers' returns among them; what its collectors caught: seconds starts a
  collector_tally watch)`.
- The tally: caught, caught_by_type and read_every; per collector caught, caught_by_type, inserters and
  taken_otherwise. Then made, made_by_type and made_minus_caught (the crushers' returns and the counts' timing).
  gone_in_reach stays as before, marked inferred; inferred_minus_caught compares it with caught. by_type gives
  {name, made, caught, made_minus_caught, inferred, inferred_minus_caught}. The old collected, collected_by_type and
  inferred_minus_collected are gone. The watch's line in status work reads `N chunks caught; M gone inside a reach
  (inferred)`.
- The same label elsewhere: platform_endurance's line `asteroid chunks collected` is now `asteroid chunks made
  (production statistics: the collectors' catch and the crushers' returns)`, and chunks_collected is now chunks_made.
  platform_digest's chunk line reads `made (collectors' catch and crushers' returns): ...`.
- Tests: tests/d24_batch143.lua (fails on main: `not called collected`); tests/d22_batch78.lua, d22_batch81.lua,
  d16_batch6.lua and platdigest.lua use the new names.

  with a circuit enable and a pole wired to it failed as above (36 ms with the dry run's other checks); the live call

## d24 batch141 PM1 (eng/d20-batch141): requests failed after its change; a reply that fails after a change (Sol #2125)
- Sol's `requests {platform: "Meridian-V", section: 23, set: [{item: "bioflux", min: 20, max: 30, from: "gleba",
  min_payload: 10}]}` (tick 55693611) set the slot, then answered `bad argument #5 of 9 to 'format' (number expected,
  got nil)`. The cause was in space.lua's sends_down: batch137's finite max sends all above it, asked or not, and the
  line named the landing pads' ask at that planet for an item they do not ask for (nil). It now reads 0.
- The game's "of N" counts stack slots, not values: the same 7-argument call read "of 8" from a function and "of 9"
  under the copy's traced pcall. The traceback on the copy put the failure in sends_down.
- The copy also showed that sends_down's per-stop rule was wrong for a platform in flight. Meridian-V, flying from
  Gleba to Nauvis with 180 bioflux, went from 180..180 to 20..30 from gleba. The 150 over the max were in its trash
  within 4 s, and all 150 went down to Nauvis's pad at the stop. The 30 stayed aboard (the pad asks 10 but then held
  the 150), and it left for Gleba with 30. The reply had said `10 down to nauvis, 140 down to gleba`.
- sends_down now first takes all the hub holds over its max for the item (the maxes of its active requests for it
  added up, any planet). That part goes to the trash now and down at the first stop, asked or not, and the pads there
  count it as held for the rest. Then batch137's rule runs as before. The reply now reads `bioflux: the hub holds 180;
  its requests would keep 30 at gleba (kept 180 at gleba): 150 over its max 30 go to the hub's trash now and down to
  nauvis at its next stop, asked or not; 30 stay aboard`. KEEP_RULE (sends_down_rule) says it with the measurement.
- Other format calls in the same code fed by a value that can be nil (no min, no max, no import planet, a quality,
  a min_payload): filter_text, the imports lines, over_max, the keep lines, construction_overlap, minpayload.lua's
  lines and shipment's stop lines all guard theirs. sends_down's pad ask was the only bare one (`.ask[` across the mod).
- A reply that fails after a change:
  - requests: each part of the reply after the change is read on its own (told_of_edit, sections, sends_down,
    trash_unrequested, on_the_way, unfilled, note, construction_requests, hub_trash). A part that fails is named with
    its error in `reply_failed`, and the rest stays. `reply_failed_note` says `the change was made (stored,
    changed_section)`, or `nothing was changed (dry run)`.
  - A dry run that fails, in its reply or before it, now puts back what it set. Before, a failure skipped the undo, and
    the dry run's change stayed.
  - made.lua: requests, platform_schedule, min_payload and drop mark each change as they make it, and are wrapped last
    in runtime.lua. A wrapped call that fails after a mark answers ok with `change_made` (each change), `reply_failed`
    (the error) and `reply_failed_note`. One that fails before any mark fails as before. The marks are each slot set,
    cleared or kept, a section added, removed, switched or emptied, a group set, the construction, trash and buffer
    switches, platform_schedule's stops/current/paused before and after, each minimum payload set, and each cargo pod
    a drop sent.
  - Checked and left alone: launch, land and platform_create build their replies from reads made before the change.
  - Also found, and fixed in cp2: platform_schedule_call's edit-log lookup checked `type(pl)=='table'`, which dropped
    every real platform (userdata), the same bug batch100 BJ1 fixed in platform_schedule. So no schedule edit (stops,
    paused, the departure gate) was recorded in the edit log on the game, and nobody was told of another agent's
    edit. The lookup now keeps whatever M.platform finds. The platform reads' last-edit lines and the tells to the last
    editor now work on the game as in the tests.
- On a headless copy of world n's 03:41 autosave (paused at tick 55693680, Meridian-V flying gleba->nauvis, hub 180):
  - before (world n's runtime): `bad argument #5 of 8 to 'format' (number expected, got nil)`, slot set to 20..30.
  - after: ok, with stored, sends_down as above, and over_max `150 over the max 30`.
  - With string.format made to fail on chosen texts: requests answered ok with `reply_failed: ["sends_down: forced test
    failure"]`, and platform_schedule answered ok with `change_made: ["Meridian-V schedule: 1 nauvis, 2 gleba, current 2
    (was ... current 1)"]`.
- Tests: tests/d24_batch141.lua (fails on main with Sol's error); tests/d17_batch31.lua's finite-max line now reads the
  trash wording, with the same counts.


## d24 batch144 PP1 (eng/d20-batch144): remove_ghosts, one's own ghosts taken away by remote view (Luna #2137)
- Luna staged a 24-ghost copy of her green circuit draft on Nauvis in (970,596)-(1004,612), charted ground no
  construction area covers, and saved it as a library blueprint. `deconstruct {dry_run}` there read would_mark 0, and
  nothing else took the ghosts back; if robot coverage grew there, robots would build the partial copy.
- In 2.0 a player in remote view removes ghosts anywhere the map is charted (the deconstruction planner over ghosts).
  `remove_ghosts {area | positions, surface? | platform?, names?, tiles?, owner?, dry_run?}` (removeghosts.lua; in
  bots.lua's PLATFORM_ACTIONS and SURFACE_ACTIONS; passive: no walk, no queue stop):
  - scope: `area` up to 256 tiles a side, or 1..64 `positions` (ghosts whose centre is within 0.5 tiles of each);
    `names` 1..32 entity or tile names; entity ghosts only, tile ghosts too with `tiles: true`. Built entities and
    tiles are never taken (the search is by type entity-ghost and tile-ghost).
  - whose: the harness's placement record (ghostlog.lua: the agent whose place_ghosts, route, paste or blueprint_place
    put it down), else the game's last user (a player's); by default only the caller's, `owner: "any"` every ghost of
    ours (`by_owner`), `owner: "sol"` only sol's. A ghost in a chunk our force has not charted stays.
  - at most 256 a call (the search stops at 4096); the ghost is destroyed with raise_destroy and its record forgotten.
  - reply: `removed` (dry run `would_remove`), `found`, `by_name`, `ghosts` (the first 64: name, tile, position,
    owner, placed; `more`), `left` with `left_others` {agent: count}, `left_unknown`, `left_uncharted`,
    `left_over_cap`, `left_why`, `capped_find`, `line`.
- ghostlog.lua: tile ghosts placed through place_ghosts `tiles` (and the routes' tile ghosts) now get a record too, in a
  ring of their own (8192, so a platform's foundation does not push out the entities' records); the key uses the tile
  name. Each record keeps its surface and a numeric position key, and a per-surface count of records at each position
  (`pidx`) lets a lookup skip ghosts with no record without turning their position into text (2.0.77 container: 8 us
  a number, 632 ghosts 10 ms). A counted record carries `x`.
- (cp2, operator: no step over 10 ms on world n) Records from before the index are counted in slices from the harness
  tick (`ghostlog.index` part), 512 ring slots a tick, the entities' ring then the tiles' (16384 slots, 32 ticks); a
  record placed meanwhile is counted when placed and skipped at its slot. Until it is whole a lookup reads the text key,
  and remove_ghosts refuses: `nothing removed: the ghost placement records are being indexed after a harness update
  (3072 of 16384 record slots read, 512 a tick, about 0.4 s left); remove_ghosts answers once that is done`.
- Measured:
  - world n (tick 55927300, d24 04:46): the search remove_ghosts makes over Luna's staging area, as a
    /silent-command read: 24 entity ghosts (8 fast-transport-belt, 6 pipe, 4 medium-electric-pole, 2 bulk-inserter,
    2 fast-inserter, 1 foundry, 1 passive-provider-chest), chunk charted, 0.25 ms. Luna's own `ghosts` reads there
    say `ghost by luna (place_ghosts, a call)` for each. No save was made for this one read.
  - headless copy of world n's 04:42 autosave (pog-b144-headless, this branch deployed): sol's call left all 24
    (`left_others {luna: 24}`); luna's dry run would remove 24; her live call removed 24 (8 fast-transport-belt, 6
    pipe, 4 medium-electric-pole, 2 bulk-inserter, 2 fast-inserter, 1 foundry, 1 passive-provider-chest), and a read
    after found no ghost and the area's 22 neutral trees in place. A mixed case on the same ground (luna's 4
    stone-wall ghosts and 4 concrete tile ghosts, sol's wall ghost, a built wooden chest): luna's default took the 4
    walls, `tiles: true` the concrete too, `owner: "sol"` sol's wall, `positions` with `names` one wall; the chest
    stayed. On platform Chalk, 2 script ghosts (no record) stayed under luna's default call (`left_unknown 2`) and went
    with `owner: "any"`.
  - cost on the copy (handler alone, mean of 10): Vulcanus's densest 256x256 square (632 ghosts, none recorded,
    tiles: true) 1.8 ms own, 1.9 ms any, from 25 ms before the position index; Luna's staging area 0.04 ms. Whole
    dispatches in the emulated container varied 3-25 ms for `clock` alone.
  - (cp2) the index build on a fresh copy of world n's 05:13 autosave (tick 56016264: 7927 entity records, none with
    a position key, 0 tile records): after the deploy it was whole 32 ticks later (index sum 7927 = records); each
    512-slot slice timed alone, 3 runs: worst 3.0 ms (2.6, 3.0, 3.0), median 1.3 ms, 28-32 ms in all; the tiles' ring
    slices (empty) under 0.1 ms. In the harness tick under profile_ticks: 32 ticks, 27.5 ms in all (0.86 ms a tick).
    A ring holds at most 8192 records, so no slice reads more than 512 whatever the log's size.
- Test: tests/d24_batch144.lua (refusals, dry run and live by owner, unknown, uncharted, names, positions, tile ghosts,
  owner "sol" and "any", the 256 cap, an old log indexed in 32 slices with the refusal meanwhile and a placement
  during it counted once, the index against the records after removals and after the ring wraps).
- Tests: tests/d24_batch141.lua (fails on main with Sol's error; its cp2 block, a userdata platform's schedule edit
